combo-voters-and-charter.essay:
In a democracy a small group of new residents can outvote a very small town. The idea is to move enough people to a place to control its government, then use that control to get a charter, which is the founding document of a city, on your own terms. It combines the takeover of a town, a claim inside a state, and a local version of the host's carve-out. In the United States, a city's charter can set its own form of government, though in many states a city has only those powers the state gives it.

The law is clear on the basic steps. Anyone may move, and residents may vote. In the 1982 Antelope vote, Rajneesh's followers had moved in and defeated a plan by older residents to dissolve the town, and that was lawful. The Free State Project gathered about 6,232 movers to New Hampshire by May 2022, and 17 of them held seats in its 400-member House in 2017 to 2018. The Free Town Project in Grafton from 2004 pushed through a 30 percent budget cut in a town of about 1,300. Starbase, Texas, incorporated in May 2025 by a vote under ordinary state rules, with a SpaceX vice-president unopposed as mayor. Nothing about these steps was illegal in itself. A court in the Vernon, California, case in 2006 found that newcomers had received free rent and jobs before registering, and ruled that those actions were not illegal.

Criminal law sets the limit. In 1984 the Rajneeshees poisoned salad bars at ten restaurants with salmonella, sickening 751 people, to lower turnout in county elections, and they bused in upwards of 4,000 homeless people in part to add voters. Those acts led to prosecutions and the end of the commune. Similarly, the state can always respond. The charter itself comes from state law, the state can change that law, and Florida's 2022 and 2023 laws on Reedy Creek show how fast that can happen. California's Assembly voted 58 to 7 in 2011 to dissolve Vernon, and the state Senate rejected the bill on 29 August 2011 after the city agreed to reforms.

What is open is where the rules stop for a group that moved for a shared purpose. A court may ask whether a person really lives somewhere, and this varies by state and by facts. Reading the record, it seems that a group's shared purpose is not unlawful in itself, and that the questions arise when residence is fake or when a town serves one religion, as in the Kiryas Joel case and at Rajneeshpuram. Americans also disagree about whether a small group should be able to use local rules this way. Older residents of Antelope tried to dissolve their own town to prevent it, and the people who moved said they were using their rights. The Free State Project's own founder, Jason Sorens, outlined a secessionist movement in his first essay of July 2001 and moved away from secession in a follow-up two weeks later.

Follow the sequence. First comes recruitment and a choice of town, which is usually very small because that takes fewer voters. People need housing, jobs and schools for their children, and the shortage of these is what caps the numbers. Then the group contests elections and is met with suspicion and with lawsuits. In Grafton the newcomers' own lawsuits raised town costs. If the group wins, it can change local taxes and zoning, within state law. It cannot change federal law, state criminal law or who issues a passport. Its bonds and contracts remain subject to courts. A mayor of a small town also finds that the state's rules on merging towns, and its tax and police rules, are still in force, as Filettino's mayor did in Italy in 2011. Killington in Vermont voted at a town meeting in 2004 to leave for New Hampshire, and it is still in Vermont.

It has real potential as local politics. A very small group can control a very small town, sometimes for decades. The strongest version moves many households with good reasons to stay, acts within election law, gets a charter under general law, and picks a state that gives its cities broad powers. That can bring local rules on land use, some taxes and the running of services. It cannot bring separation from the country, and it brings neighbours' attention with it.

combo-bankrupt-village.essay:
News stories regularly announce that a whole town has been sold. The idea built on this is to buy a failing village, or a government in financial trouble, and thereby acquire the place and the power that runs it. It combines a purchase, a takeover of a town, and a claim inside a state.

What can be bought and what cannot is settled. A town consists of private land parcels, plus a municipal government where one exists. A person can buy all the parcels. A public government has no owner, so no one can buy it. Buford, Wyoming, is the best-known sale. On 5 April 2012 Don Sammons sold it at auction for $900,000 to two Vietnamese men, one later named as Pham Dinh Nguyen. What they bought was about 10 acres of private land with a trading post and gas station, and Buford was an unincorporated community within Albany County, which continued to govern it. The buyer rebranded it PhinDeli Town in 2013, the store was boarded up in 2017, and by 2021 the fuel station was back in business.

Bankruptcy gives no further opening in the United States. Chapter 9 of the federal bankruptcy code is the process for a municipality that cannot pay its debts. Section 109(c) says that an entity may use it only if it is a municipality, is specifically authorised by state law to do so, is insolvent and meets further conditions. In other words the state keeps control over who may enter bankruptcy. A court then helps the municipality adjust its debts, and there is no auction of the government. Other countries respond to failing towns by merging them. Italy's austerity plan of 2011 called for towns under 1,000 people to merge with neighbours, which is what led Filettino's mayor to declare a principality in protest, and how towns are organised was still decided by the Italian parliament.

What is open is less about law and more about what a very small population lets an owner do in practice. Owning all the homes in a real municipality, as Vernon's city government did with its housing, gives great influence over who lives and votes there. Whether a new private owner could use this to direct a local government depends on state law on evictions, voting and fair housing. In one Vernon election the city cut off the power of challengers and a judge stepped in. Reading the record, it seems that the combination of very few voters and one landlord is effective, and that it draws state attention once it is noticed.

History does contain true sales of a ruler's rights after money trouble, and they show why the modern version does not work. Before 1699 an imperial commission decided that Schellenberg and Vaduz, whose counts were in debt, should be sold to clear their debts, and the Liechtenstein family bought them. Those were personal lordships, which could be sold under the imperial law of that time. The fief of Sark has also changed hands by sale, and still has a very old structure, yet it answers to the British Crown. In 2010 German politicians suggested that Greece, in its debt crisis, sell islands, and Greece did not. A government in debt might sell land and state companies, while keeping the right to rule.

Follow the steps. A buyer finds an empty village on a listing. It pays for the land, and the sale is entered in the public land register. Any old buildings come with liabilities, and the buyer pays local property tax. The local council, or the county, has planning control. Bringing in residents needs water, sewers and permits, which is why many such villages are empty. A buyer who declares independence, as Seborga's claimant has done since 1963 and Romkerhall's innkeepers have done for tourists, gets publicity and possibly visitors, while the state carries on running the place. A small place that declares it and then refuses taxes faces the same collection system as anyone else.

The potential is modest and real. The strongest version is a group that buys an entire near-empty place in a country with few rules on such purchases, brings in residents, and forms or takes over the local government in a lawful way, using the voters-and-charter route. That gives a physical home, control of planning and a lot of practical freedom. It gives no more legal separation from the country than that route gives.

combo-two-state-condominium.essay:
A condominium, in international law, is a territory shared and governed by two or more powers at once. It usually settles a quarrel when neither side will give up its claim. The idea here is that two states, perhaps neighbours with a shared problem, could set up a jointly run zone under an authority of their own, with a private project inside it. Each would check the other, and neither alone could cancel it. This combines an international agreement, a buffer between states and a carve-out.

There are many real examples. The New Hebrides were run jointly by France and Britain from 1906 until independence in 1980 as Vanuatu. Neutral Moresnet, 3.5 square kilometres, was run by commissioners from the Netherlands and then Belgium and from Prussia from 1816 to 1920 because both wanted its zinc mine. The mine company dominated daily life, running housing, shops, a hospital and a bank, and residents counted as stateless. Pheasant Island in the Bidasoa river changes hands between Spain and France every six months. The Moselle is a condominium of Germany and Luxembourg. Lake Titicaca's waters were declared an indivisible condominium of Peru and Bolivia. Under a 1973 treaty, Brazil and Paraguay created a binational entity called ITAIPU to run the Paraná River's hydroelectric power, and Argentina and Uruguay share the Río de la Plata's jurisdiction under another treaty of 1973.

Two more modern designs matter most for a project. EuroAirport Basel Mulhouse Freiburg lies in France, opened in 1946 and is jointly run by France and Switzerland under an international convention of 1949, with a customs-free road of about 2.5 kilometres, built from 1951 to 1953, linking it to Basel. The Nigeria and São Tomé and Príncipe Joint Development Authority was created by a treaty signed on 21 February 2001 to regulate a shared seabed zone thought to hold oil and gas. Its history shows the risks. It is reported to have raised $300 million in signature bonuses, yet by 2018 it had funding problems and could not pay staff for months, and Nigeria had earlier considered withdrawing.

What is settled is that two states can do this, and that only states can. Treaties between states create the authority, and it carries only what they give it. A private body may run a mine or a dam under such an authority, but it holds no share of the sovereignty. Also settled is that the states can end it together, or that one can leave if the treaty says so. Neutral Moresnet ended when the Treaty of Versailles gave it to Belgium. The Brčko District shows a condominium-type solution within a single country.

What is open is the status of people in such a place. Moresnet's residents were stateless, with no passports of their own, and modern human rights law would treat that differently. No general treaty explains how to handle a condominium's nationality, tax or courts, so each document must say so. Moresnet's mine doctor, Wilhelm Molly, proposed in 1908 turning it into an Esperanto-speaking state called Amikejo, and nothing came of that, and a casino that opened in 1903 closed after pressure from the German emperor. Reading these cases, it seems that the neighbours' joint control gives stability against one of them acting alone, and that it also gives each of them a veto, so that innovations are hard to get.

Follow what a modern founder would meet. Two foreign ministries would need a reason to work together, and a founder's project would rarely be one on its own. Disputes over a border or shared resources are the usual motive, so the founder would be stepping into a quarrel. Each state's parliament would ratify the treaty, and each state's constitution might limit it. Each would also want its police and courts to have some role. Banks would likely want to know whose regulator and whose central bank are responsible. Staff would have the nationality of one or other side, and the two states' laws might conflict. The arrangement can go on unchanged for a long time when both sides are content, and the risk arrives when relations between the two worsen, as a joint authority has no independent force.

The strongest version would be a modest economic zone on a border, under a treaty that gives a joint authority clear legal personality, with a private operator on a long contract. Such a place could offer a mix of rules unavailable in either country, as a bi-national airport does. It would remain the shared property of two states, and it would have two governments to answer to in place of one.

combo-floating-host-zone.essay:
Most people picture a floating settlement far out at sea. A different plan is to float one near shore, inside a country's waters, with that country's agreement and a special legal framework. This combines the territorial sea or the exclusive economic zone with the host's carve-out. It gives up the attempt to escape the coastal state, in exchange for calm water, a nearby port and a government partner.

The law of the sea is clear on the framework. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, gives a coastal state sovereignty in its territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles, or about 22 kilometres, from its coast. Beyond it, out to 200 nautical miles, lies the exclusive economic zone, where Article 60 gives the coastal state the exclusive right to build and to authorise artificial islands and certain installations, and exclusive legal power over them, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law. So a host can permit a floating zone and set its rules. Without permission, a long-term structure is at risk. Thailand's navy raided the XLII seastead 14 nautical miles off Phuket in 2019, and Thai officials raised the possibility of the death penalty, on a charge of violating sovereignty.

One gap remains in UNCLOS. It does not define artificial island, and it does not say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. A structure that stays in place and houses people looks more like what Article 60 covers, but no international court has decided this, and no court outcome in the XLII case is known. The couple living there were not caught. With a host agreement the gap matters less, because the host has already said yes. It matters when a host's successor later changes its mind or when a third country's ship wants to pass.

The real attempts all turned on politics and money. On 13 January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the Seasteading Institute for studies toward seazones with a special governing framework. A memorandum records intentions and usually binds no one. Local people objected, the opposition demanded withdrawal, and in February 2018 the government's position was reported that the deal had no legal force and had expired at the end of 2017. In the Maldives, the government signed with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010, and signed again in 2019 and 2022 after a change of government, for a housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon near Malé. Reports differ on how much has been built. At Busan in South Korea, the city, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX signed in November 2021 to build a prototype, with about $200 million anticipated and with South Korean law applying to property, police and courts. A local report in October 2023 said no concrete financing had been presented. Kiribati's president spoke in 2011 of floating islands costing about $2 billion, to come from other countries.

What is open, and what has not been tested, is how far a host can go. A country that has authority over its waters could in principle pass a statute giving a floating zone its own commercial law, in the same way as a zone on land. Whether a French territory, for example, could have done so without Paris is something no court has had to decide for this project. Reading UNCLOS, it seems that a coastal state may delegate management inside its waters, and that it cannot pass on its international position, since other states' rights of passage and navigation, and the coastal state's duties, run to the state itself.

Follow the steps. The first is a site study and a set of letters. Next comes a law, which means a public debate, with fishermen and neighbours among those heard. Marine engineers and insurers then want storm data and a classification society's approval, and lenders want the land-law equivalent of a title, which water cannot provide unless the host's law creates one. Boats, ports, medical care and supplies come from the host. A birth or a will on the platform runs under host law, as the host has authority. Environmental review of a lagoon may be the point at which the plan stops. Each change of government reopens the deal, as the Maldives shows.

The most workable version is close to what Busan proposed, which is new floating housing under the ordinary law of a willing host, perhaps with a modest economic zone added. It can answer real needs, particularly for low islands with rising seas, and it can be built with existing engineering at high cost. It gives no separation. A floating city under such an agreement is a neighbourhood of that country, and its residents remain under its law.

combo-treaty-buffer-land.essay:
Buffer zones exist because two sides have stopped fighting without settling who owns what, and a strip of land is kept between them. Some people see these as gaps in the world's map. This route asks whether a treaty could turn such a strip, or a demilitarised area, into a place for a community or a special regime. It combines a buffer zone with international agreement and a host's consent.

The first thing the law settles is that a buffer is not empty of claims. The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, 346 square kilometres, was set by ceasefire, and the UN patrols it without owning it, while the claims of the governments on either side continue. Korea's Demilitarized Zone, about 250 kilometres long and 4 wide, comes from the armistice of 27 July 1953. Two villages remain inside it by decision of the armistice committee. Daeseong-dong on the southern side is protected by the United Nations Command, and its 218 residents in 2008 were South Korean citizens who paid no tax and did no military service, on condition that they spend 240 nights a year there. A person arriving there could not join them, since residence descends from pre-war landowners. Pyla in Cyprus is a mixed village in the zone, and estimates of the people living in the Cyprus zone differ, from some 10,000 to about 14,000 if the listed 2021 populations of its four villages are added up.

A peace treaty can do more. The Israel and Jordan treaty of 1994 recognised Jordanian sovereignty at Baqura, also called Naharayim or the Island of Peace, and it gave Israeli landowners who had held the land since before 1948 a special regime with free entry at no charge. The annex that set this up lasted 25 years and renewed automatically unless one side gave a year's notice, and reports often call it a lease. Jordan gave that notice in October 2018 and took full control on 10 November 2019. The Åland Islands are the longest-running peaceful example of demilitarisation. They are neutral under a 1921 convention and part of Finland. The Free Territory of Trieste was the grand design, to be a neutral country under the UN Security Council, and it never got past military governors before Italy and Yugoslavia divided it in 1954.

Now the open points. Nobody has decided whether a third party could administer a demilitarised strip for residents under a new treaty, because no one has asked. In Moresnet and Brčko, a joint regime emerged from a dispute, and each was the work of the parties. Reading the examples, it seems that any such regime needs consent from both of the parties whose quarrel made the buffer. Those parties have often not been able to agree on more basic things. No case has tested whether the UN or another body could accept such a job for a private community.

Follow it step by step. A private group arriving in a UN buffer zone would be stopped by peacekeepers or by the armed forces at the edges. In Korea, the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world. Suppose the two parties wanted a neutral project, say a peace park or a free economic zone. A founder would need both to sign, and a treaty term with an end date or a notice clause, of the kind Jordan used. Investors and insurers would see that one bad year in relations could shut it. Its residents would keep their nationality, its goods would have to pass through one or both sides' customs, and any bank would look to those two states. If the regime ended, private rights would rest on whatever the treaty says. At Baqura, Jordan took full control when the regime ended. The annex had protected private ownership during its term and did not say what would happen to ownership after it ended.

The potential is low, and it is tied to peace-making. The strongest version is a treaty that ends a dispute and includes a special area, with clear rights for those already on the land, under a body both sides trust. Such a place could bring real benefit to its people. A founder's role in it would be small, as a contractor or investor at most, and the sovereignty questions would be settled by the two states.

combo-leased-private-operator.essay:
Governments sometimes lease a port or a zone to a foreign company for a very long time. Long terms like 99 years invite people to treat these places as outposts, and a founder might hope for the same. The idea combines a long lease with the purchase route and a carve-out, with a private operator in place of a foreign government. A comparison with the Panama Canal Zone shows the difference between running a port and governing land.

The modern cases are plainly commercial, and that much is settled. In October 2015 the Northern Territory government in Australia gave Landbridge, a privately held Chinese company, a 99-year lease of the Port of Darwin for A$506 million. In July 2017 Sri Lanka's ports authority signed a 99-year lease of Hambantota's port with China Merchants Port for $1.12 billion, through a joint company, with a 15,000-acre economic zone also provided for. Sources give the company's share as either 70 or 85 percent. Neither lease moved sovereignty. Australian and Sri Lankan law still apply. In Laos, the Hong Kong-registered company in the Golden Triangle has 99 years on 10,000 hectares and its own immigration checkpoint, and that is on Lao soil. These leases hand over the operating of a business and a place.

The Canal Zone was a different legal thing. By a convention proclaimed in 1904, the United States received use, occupation and control of a strip of 1,432 square kilometres in perpetuity, and it ran its own governor, police, courts and judges. Panama's grant came straight after the American government had helped it become independent. None of the modern private leases described here carries such powers. Even that grant ended, with the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, the end of the zone on 1 October 1979 and of the canal's joint running on 31 December 1999. It had caused riots in 1958, 1959 and 1964. A grant written to last forever ran for 75 years.

Recent events show how a host can undo a long lease. Reviews in 2021 and 2023 found no grounds to cancel Darwin's lease. In April 2025 the Australian prime minister said the country wanted to buy it back, both main parties promised to return it, and in January 2026 China's ambassador warned against the plan. On 24 April 2026 Landbridge filed a claim at ICSID, saying Australia's actions were discriminatory. In Panama, Hutchison's company ran the Balboa and Cristobal ports from the 1990s, and its contract renewed for 25 years in 2021. The Supreme Court ruled the contracts unconstitutional on 29 January 2026, after a suit brought the year before during American pressure on Panama. Reports in February 2026 said the government ordered the ports occupied, and the company has since claimed losses of more than $2 billion in arbitration. In Solomon Islands, the Tulagi deal of 2019 died within weeks because a province had no power to make it.

What is open is first of all about motive. At Hambantota, critics called the lease a debt trap. The payment was mostly used to pay other debts, and scholars including Brautigam and Brown dispute that account, with Brown arguing that China took on more risk and got entangled in local politics. The second open question is how far an international tribunal can reach, as in Darwin. Neither has been resolved. Sri Lanka's foreign minister called the lease a mistake in 2021, and the deal stands.

Follow what a private founder would face. The founder needs serious money first, because these deals cost from hundreds of millions of dollars upward. Next is a bidding process, which is often public, and security reviews at home and in the host. A port needs an operating record, cranes and shipping lines, and insurers will want one. The operator would pay local tax, unless a special law exempts it, employ local people, and follow local customs law. Police and courts remain the host's. People on the land have no new nationality. A home-country government may also be pulled in. The Hutchison sale to a BlackRock-led consortium stalled over objections from the Chinese government, which shows that a company's home state can have a say as well.

The strongest version is what these operators do have. It is a well-capitalised company with a concession under clear law and a treaty behind it, and a host that keeps getting benefits. That gives a long period of operating control over valuable land, and often a say in what is built there. It is a useful commercial position. It is not, and has not been in any modern case, a path to ruling people or leaving the host's legal order. Reading the leases and the rulings, it seems that the longer and larger the lease, the more it draws political attention to its strategic importance.

combo-private-force.essay:
Every attempt to claim land eventually meets the question of who will defend it. A group with money can hire armed men, and there is a long history of doing so. The idea combines a takeover, an unrecognised state and a private security or military company as the means of holding ground. The first thing to understand is that the law treats this as a crime in many places, and that it follows people home.

Several rules are clear. In the United States, 18 U.S.C. § 960 says that whoever, within the country, knowingly begins, sets on foot, prepares a means for, furnishes money for or takes part in a military expedition against a foreign state or people with whom the United States is at peace faces a fine and up to three years in prison. This is the descendant of the Neutrality Act of 1794, and it was used in the Gambian coup attempt of 2014. Cherno Njie, a Texas developer who financed the plot, was sentenced to a year and a day, and others to six months or time served. In Britain, the Foreign Enlistment Act 1870 makes it unlawful for British subjects to join forces of a state at war with a state at peace with Britain. South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act of 1998 bans citizens and residents from taking part in foreign conflicts without a government committee's approval, and France's 2003 law makes mercenary activity a crime for its citizens, residents and companies.

Internationally, Article 47 of Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, adopted in 1977, says that a mercenary has no right to be a combatant or a prisoner of war, though humane treatment and a trial are still required. The definition requires six things together, including being specially recruited, taking a direct part in fighting and being paid much more than regular soldiers. The UN Mercenary Convention, adopted on 4 December 1989 and in force since 20 October 2001, has a broader rule covering foreigners recruited to overthrow a government for private gain, even if they take no direct part in fighting. Most countries, including the United States and Britain, have not joined it.

The real open question is the line between lawful security and an unlawful force. Hired guards are legal in most places. A private company may guard a mine or a port, and Executive Outcomes, which was founded in South Africa in 1989, had large companies among its clients and worked for the governments of Angola and Sierra Leone. It is said to have received a licence under South Africa's 1998 act, a point that is poorly documented, and the act required approval for military help abroad, so the case gives little guidance on whether work for a recognised government is treated differently from work against one. Whether a guard force holding land for a private founder against a host's police counts as a mercenary or just as criminals depends on the facts and on national law, and few tests exist. The definition is narrow, since all six conditions must be met, and some countries, including the United States, do not endorse it. Reading the text, it seems that a force holding unclaimed land, in the absence of an armed conflict, might not fit Article 47 at all, and that this gives no protection, since ordinary criminal law applies when any state acts.

The history shows a predictable arc. Mike Hoare's force of 1981 went to the Seychelles disguised as rugby players, was detected at the airport and fled in a hijacked plane, and many were tried in South Africa. Bob Denard took over the Comoros with 43 men in 1978 and ran its presidential guard for 11 years, which is the nearest thing to a long success, with outside backing from France and others. He too was forced out. Simon Mann's Wonga Coup plot of 2004 was stopped when Zimbabwean police impounded a Boeing 727 at Harare where weapons were to be loaded. Executive Outcomes retook Sierra Leone's diamond fields in 1995, then withdrew under international pressure. It dissolved on 31 December 1998, the year South Africa's act passed. At Sealand in 1978, hired men took the fort and the family retook it by helicopter, and Germany then called the episode an act of piracy.

Follow the indirect routes. Guns must be bought, and export control laws cover them and the parts, so sellers need licences. Pilots need flight plans, and aircraft are registered in a state. Money for a force moves through banks with reporting duties, and the Wonga plot's payments were later traced through bank records. Recruits are nationals of some country, and their home state may prosecute them. Insurers will not cover an illegal expedition. Once on the land, the group is on someone's territory, and it can be treated as an invading force, with no prisoner of war status. The UN Charter's ban on force protects states, and not a private camp. If a warship arrives at a platform, a private force can do little.

Force has so far brought small groups short periods of control, and it has never brought recognition on its own. The strongest lawful version is a licensed guard company protecting a lawful project with the host's agreement, under the host's law. That is ordinary security. An armed attempt to hold land against a state would mean crimes for everyone involved, from the funder to the driver.

combo-flag-theory.essay:
Flag theory is an idea for getting many of the things a private country promises without owning any land. A person places each part of their life under a different country, so that no single government holds all of it. The idea is credited to the investment writer Harry D. Schultz, who proposed three "flags": a second passport, an address in a tax haven, and assets kept outside the home country. It later grew to five, adding a place to run a business and a place to spend money. In the 1980s and 1990s a British company, Scope International, sold books under the name W.G. Hill, possibly a pseudonym, describing the "perpetual traveller". This is someone who keeps moving and never stays long enough to count as a legal resident anywhere, in the hope of owing no income tax, military service or jury duty.

It helps to separate this from founding a territory. Nothing is claimed and no flag is raised. The combination is made of ordinary legal products from real states, which is why no navy has any reason to act against it. The person gets choice among governments and gives up any claim to a place of their own.

Some of the law here is settled. Each country decides who its nationals are. Each country also decides who owes it tax, and the common test is residence, usually looking at days present, a home, family and work. The United States is the large exception. It taxes citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, and the Supreme Court upheld this in Cook v. Tait in 1924 for a citizen living in Mexico. So an American cannot become a perpetual traveller by travelling. The only exit is giving up citizenship, which carries a fee and, for people above set wealth or tax thresholds or behind on their filings, an exit tax treating their assets as sold the day before they leave.

The second settled change is in the banks. Under FATCA, the American law, foreign banks report US account holders to the tax agency. Under the Common Reporting Standard, an international system run through the OECD, banks in the countries and territories that have adopted it collect each customer's tax home and governments swap the data. The group that oversees this, the Global Forum, has about 172 members, and not every member has adopted this exchange. A report from that group gives 171 million accounts. Suppose a traveller opens an account in a low-tax country and tells the bank "I am tax resident nowhere". The bank has to ask for a tax residence and for proof of it, and an answer it cannot record invites refusal or further questions. The third flag, assets kept abroad out of sight, depended on banks saying nothing, and for most people with ordinary accounts that has ended.

The OECD has also said that certain residence and citizenship by investment schemes may be misused to hide offshore assets, and it monitors what it treats as high-risk schemes. A purchased residence certificate from a low-tax island is therefore something a bank may look at with more suspicion, whatever the paper says.

What remains open is narrower than the old books suggested. Reading the rules as they stand, it seems that no treaty obliges a person to be tax resident somewhere. Each country asks only whether the person is resident there, so a person who truly fails every country's test may owe income tax to none of them. Whether a given person has truly left is decided separately by each country, and home countries can argue that ties remain. That is a question of fact, argued case by case, and there is no international court where a traveller can get one binding answer. The honest position is that being nowhere is possible on paper and hard to prove to the people who ask, such as banks, landlords and immigration officers.

Follow it through a real week. A clinic asks for health cover, and a health insurer wants a country of residence. A child needs a school and a birth record. Staying more than a visitor's allowance needs a visa, and working during the stay needs a permit, so the person lives by the rules of each host in turn. If something goes wrong, the only government with a duty to help is the passport country, and only as far as its own consular practice goes.

The strongest version is modest. A person who is not American holds two real nationalities, keeps one real tax residence in a low-tax country where they spend real time, runs a company somewhere reputable, and reports honestly. That is legal in many cases. A community of such people could gather on a ship or in a rented town, and every member would still sit under the law of the place they are standing and of each country that issued them a document. As a route to sovereignty it gives none. As a way of lowering how much any one state can reach, it does work to a limited degree, as long as the person accepts that every flag can be withdrawn by the state that issued it. Roger Ver, who gave up US citizenship in 2014 after obtaining citizenship of Saint Kitts and Nevis, shows the limit. He was arrested in Spain in April 2024 on a US indictment over tax, and in October 2025 he agreed to pay $49.9 million under a deferred prosecution agreement.

combo-renounce-stateless.essay:
Some people who want to live outside every country try to do it with their own legal status instead of with land. They give up their citizenship and hold no other, then say they belong to a new community or to the world. The idea combines the legal act of renouncing a nationality with a replacement identity supplied by a micronation, an online nation or a world citizens' registry. To follow what this does, it helps to know what nationality is for. A nationality is the legal tie that gives a person a government obliged to take them back and entitled to speak up for them abroad. Border systems assume everyone has one.

Two treaties deal with people who have none. The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons defines a stateless person as someone "not considered as a national by any State under the operation of its law". It gives such a person certain rights in countries that have joined it, and Article 28 tells those countries to issue travel documents to stateless people lawfully staying in their territory. Article 32 asks them to make naturalisation easier as far as they can. The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness tries to stop the condition arising. Article 7(1)(a) says that where a member state's law allows renunciation, renouncing shall not end a person's nationality unless the person has or acquires another one.

That settles some things plainly. A self-declared nation is not a state, so its citizenship does not stop a person being stateless, and it gives no second nationality in the sense these treaties mean. In a country that has joined the 1961 treaty and applied it, a person trying to renounce into nothing should be refused. The treaties also give no right to enter anywhere. Article 28 applies to people already lawfully staying, and the 1954 treaty says nothing that obliges a state to admit a stateless stranger.

Not every country has joined, and the United States has long allowed a person to renounce without holding another nationality, while warning that the person will lack any government's protection and may have difficulty travelling. So the door is open in some places. Garry Davis walked through it on 25 May 1948 at the American embassy in Paris, saying he was a citizen of the world. He founded a registry in 1949 and the World Government of World Citizens in 1953, and he issued his own World Passport from about that time. He lived with no nationality for 65 years, until his death in 2013, and he was regularly arrested and expelled. He had a public profile and supporters, which most people who bought his passports did not.

Suppose a person does this today. On the day after renunciation the person is a foreigner in whatever country they stand in, with no passport and no right to stay. The host may tolerate them, grant a stay and travel document if it follows the 1954 treaty, or try to remove them. Removal is hard, since no country must take the person, and this is how people end up held in detention or stuck in transit. Mehran Karimi Nasseri, who had no accepted papers, began living in a French airport terminal in 1988. France granted him residency in 1999, he refused to sign the papers because they listed him as Iranian, and he stayed until 2006. Everyday life then gets narrower. Banks must identify customers and record a tax residence and a nationality. Employers must check a right to work. Airlines refuse boarding to someone a destination will not admit, since they carry the cost of returning them. Marriage, inheritance and registering a child all ask for documents. Article 1 of the 1961 treaty helps the next generation in one way, requiring a member state to give nationality, at birth or on application, to a person born in its territory who would otherwise be stateless, so a child may not inherit the condition, depending on where the birth happens.

Tax does not disappear either. Most countries tax by residence, so a stateless person living somewhere pays there. The former country may pursue earlier debts. The US exit tax applies to the wealthy and to those behind on filings regardless of what happens next.

What is open is whether a person may refuse all nationalities as a matter of right. Article 7(1)(b) of the 1961 treaty contains an exception, saying the bar on renouncing does not apply where it would be inconsistent with the principles of Articles 13 and 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which concern movement and asylum. That wording seems aimed at people fleeing persecution. Reading the text, it does not seem to create a general right to be stateless by choice. No court ruling on that exact question is known. It is also an open point how far a host must help someone who made themselves stateless on purpose, since the 1954 definition asks only whether any state counts the person as a national and says nothing about how it happened. On its face that covers a voluntary case, and states may read it more narrowly in practice.

The potential is small and personal. The strongest version is a person with a tolerant host that has joined the 1954 treaty, who renounces in a country that allows it, obtains a stateless person's travel document, and lives on it. That person then depends on one host's goodwill, which is more dependent than before. For a community the idea gives nothing to build on. Each member would lose the consular help, travel rights and proof of identity that other routes rely on.

combo-cbi-private-community.essay:
Citizenship by investment is a programme in which a country grants its nationality in return for a payment or investment. A private community is a town, estate or zone run by a company or association under contract with its residents. Stacking the two means that a group of like-minded people each buy the same small country's passport, or arrange a deal with that country, and then live together on private land there. The appeal is that they would hold a real nationality, with a real seat at the United Nations behind it, and live by their own contract rules, with the state at a distance because it was paid to stay friendly. No new state is founded, and the group lives under one that already exists.

The first thing that is settled is that a country may grant its nationality on its own terms, as a matter of its own law. A passport bought this way is a real passport. The second settled point comes from the International Court of Justice in Nottebohm, a 1955 case. Friedrich Nottebohm, a German who had lived in Guatemala since 1905, obtained Liechtenstein nationality during a short visit to Europe in 1939. Liechtenstein later sued Guatemala on his behalf, and the Court held the claim inadmissible. Nationality granted without a genuine connection did not entitle Liechtenstein to protect him against Guatemala, the country where he actually lived. The Court did not say the nationality was void inside Liechtenstein. So a bought passport works for travel where states accept it, and it may not give the person a government able to press a claim against their long-time country of residence.

The third settled point is new and applies within Europe. On 29 April 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in Commission v Malta, case C-181/23, that Malta had broken EU law by running a scheme that gave nationality through a transactional procedure in exchange for set payments. The Court called this the commercialisation of nationality and, through it, of EU citizenship. It relied on Article 20 of the EU's founding treaty on citizenship, on the duty of cooperation among member states and on the relationship of solidarity and good faith between a state and its nationals. Malta had argued that EU law requires no prior genuine link and that Nottebohm could not supply such a rule. The Court did not make a genuine link the test. It found the breach in the scheme's transactional nature. So the ruling closes this route for EU member states. It does not bind Caribbean or Pacific programmes.

Those programmes depend on outsiders in another way. Much of a passport's value is its visa-free access. The European Commission proposed suspending the visa waiver for Vanuatu over its scheme, which charged about $130,000. The Commission pointed to a very low rejection rate and to citizenship granted to people listed in Interpol's databases, and in March 2022 the EU Council suspended the waiver for holders of ordinary Vanuatu passports issued since 25 May 2015. The partner state can hold firm and its passport can still lose value overnight. The OECD monitors high-risk schemes because they can be used to get around bank reporting. A bank may therefore ask a holder for proof of real ties.

The Comoros shows a third way this can fail. Around a decade before 2018 the Comoros Islands agreed with the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait to sell citizenship to stateless people in those countries, known as Bidoon, in return for development money. In 2018 its parliament reported that nearly 48,000 foreigners had received passports, that thousands were sold outside official channels by what it called mafia networks, and that up to $100 million had gone missing. When a small state sells nationality in bulk, the buyers depend on that state's own honesty and politics.

Now suppose the community stage. A group of 2,000 people buys the passports of an island country and buys private land there. They write a contract covering rules of the estate, private arbitration and shared services. On the estate, ordinary property and contract law gives them a good deal of freedom, as in a large condominium or gated town. But criminal law, immigration, tax, building rules and the courts all remain the state's. Being citizens gives them something foreigners lack, which is the right to stay and a right to vote, so a group of that size in a very small country could become politically important. Reading the rules of ordinary democracy, it seems such a group could lawfully try to elect representatives and seek a special law. The Free State Project and the takeover of Antelope, Oregon, by followers of Rajneesh show how moving voters can work and how it can provoke a response. Whether local voters would tolerate a bought-in bloc is a political question nobody can answer in advance.

The state's position is the open part. Nothing in international law stops a small state from giving such a community a special zone, and a later government can reverse it. Honduras's Supreme Court struck down its zone laws in 2024 with retroactive effect. Whether a state that sells its nationality to a group has any wider duty to the group is untested. Nobody has tested the full stack of mass citizenship plus a governing contract in one place.

The potential is real but limited to the level of a very favourable host deal. The strongest version is a stable small state that passes a special zone law after a real public debate, a community whose members actually move there and live there, so that Nottebohm's genuine connection grows over time, and an investment treaty behind the zone. The support of the country's own voters would decide how long it lasts. The group would get strong autonomy under a real flag, and a later law could end it.

combo-e-residency-entity.essay:
A digital community has a problem when it wants to own anything. It has members and ideas, and no legal person that can sign a lease, hold a bank account or be sued. One answer combines two things that real states already sell to foreigners. The first is e-residency, a digital identity a state gives to non-citizens so that they can sign documents and run a company online. The second is a company, or a foundation, registered in that state, which acts as the legal body of the community. Members become its owners or members, and its charter becomes the community's constitution in practice.

Estonia is the leading example. It launched e-Residency at the end of 2014, and its official figures show over 144,000 e-residents from 187 countries and more than 44,000 companies. The state took in nearly €125 million from the programme in 2025. It does this for revenue and talent, and that is why the offer is reliable, since Estonia gains from keeping it open.

Some things here are settled. An e-resident is not a citizen, gets no right to live in Estonia, and holds no passport. A company formed this way is an ordinary Estonian company under Estonian company and tax law. The founder remains under the law of wherever they live. Suppose 500 people in thirty countries form a company as their community's shell. Estonian law governs the company. Each member's home country still taxes them on what they earn, and each home country's rules on foreign holdings apply to their share. If the group sells memberships with a promise of profit, securities law in every country where buyers live can apply. In 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued over securities offered for New Utopia, a nation that was never built. They had been sold over the internet and raised $24,000.

The less obvious settled part is reporting. Banks must find out who really owns and controls a company, and under the Common Reporting Standard they report accounts to the tax authorities of the owner's home. A company with hundreds of foreign members has more to explain, and a bank's compliance office may simply decline. A shell in a reputable country gets a hearing, which is more than a micronation's charter gets, and it does not guarantee an account.

Tax on the company itself is less tidy. As a general rule of tax law, many countries treat a company as resident where it is really managed, or as having a taxable presence where its people work. Reading those rules, it seems that a company run day to day by a founder in Berlin may be taxed in Germany as well as Estonia, whatever its papers say. Each country applies its own test, and the answer can differ. That is an uncertainty about facts more than about law, and many small online firms live with it.

What is open is how far this shell can stretch toward government. Nothing in Estonian company law appears designed to stop a company from calling its shareholders citizens in its own documents. Reading the law of contract, members can agree to a code of conduct, to pay dues and to take disputes to a private arbitrator. Whether a court would enforce a sanction such as expulsion with loss of assets depends on the host's company law and consumer law, and no court is known to have considered a community built this way. Whether a state would tolerate its company brand being used for a project claiming sovereignty is also untested. A state might view that as harmless or as a reputational problem, and it has ordinary powers to strike off a company or remove an e-resident's status. The Network School in Malaysia is the nearest warning, though it concerned a physical site. In July 2026 a city council revoked its business licence, citing breaches of licence conditions, after a political row about its aims, and ordered it to stop the next day.

There are real limits on what the shell can ever do. It cannot issue a nationality, so every member needs a real passport. It cannot arrest anyone or keep anyone in, and locking up a member would expose the organisers to criminal law. It cannot make treaties, because the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties covers agreements between states, and it can only sign contracts. It cannot issue money with legal force. Its radio, ships and aircraft, if it had any, would need state licences of the ordinary kind.

The potential is that of a strong club with a real legal skeleton. The strongest version is a foundation or company in a stable state with a published charter, an honest statement that membership is no nationality, independent audits, and members who pay their taxes at home. Such a body can buy land, employ staff, hold a treasury, run schools, insure members as a group where insurers agree, and last for decades, much as some churches and professional bodies do. It could also move, since a company can often be re-formed in another country. Its home state could still end the arrangement, and the members would keep their ordinary lives. Building such a body is well within reach. Becoming a state by this path has no known precedent, and no government would have to acknowledge such a claim.

combo-dao-shell.essay:
A DAO, or decentralised autonomous organisation, is a group that takes decisions and holds money through software running on a blockchain, a shared public ledger that no single person controls. Members usually vote using tokens, and the software carries out some decisions on its own. To people who want a country without land, this looks like a government already, with a written set of rules, votes, a treasury and members around the world. The combination here is that software plus a law from a real state that gives the group a legal body.

Without such a law the position is uncomfortable. In November 2024 a US federal court in California, in Samuels v. Lido DAO, found that a buyer had adequately pleaded that Lido DAO was a general partnership. In a partnership each partner can be personally liable for the whole group's debts. The court rejected the argument that the DAO was only software, saying its acts were "the actions of an entity run by people". The ruling came at an early stage of the case, and the court's finding on partners reached three large investors said to play important governance roles. It is still unclear which ordinary token holders could count as partners. Other US cases have pointed the same way, including a California ruling that a DAO's members could be treated as general partners and a federal regulator's enforcement action against Ooki DAO. So the law has not decided the outer edge, and it has made clear that calling a group software gives no shelter.

Several legislatures have offered a legal form in response. Wyoming was the first US state, in 2021, letting a DAO register as a kind of limited liability company, with a 2022 amendment allowing management by members or by algorithm. Tennessee and Vermont have also passed laws allowing DAOs to form as limited liability companies. Wyoming later added a further form. Utah's act, signed on 13 March 2023 and effective on 1 January 2024, created a distinct entity called the limited liability DAO. Members are liable only for their on-chain contributions, except that those who vote to disobey a court order can be personally liable. It must be formed by at least one natural person and show the state that its code has undergone quality assurance. The Marshall Islands, an independent country, passed a law in 2022 and a second in 2023. According to a legal commentary, the 2022 law required only one person to give identity details to the registry, and the 2023 law added series, where sub-DAOs hold separate assets and liabilities.

These laws settle something modest. A registered DAO can own property, sign contracts and limit members' liability under that jurisdiction's law. CityDAO used Wyoming's law to buy 40 acres near Cody in 2021. Its 6,500 or so "citizens" hold a token, and county zoning still applied to the land. Each law also keeps a human link, in the form of a registered person, an identifier in the filing or a named founder. A state regulator and a court therefore have someone to find. No law listed here gives a DAO any authority over land or people beyond what a company has.

The Marshall Islands law raises the most interesting grey point. It comes from a recognised state, so the entity is a real legal person. Series DAOs resemble a federation of provinces on paper. Reading the idea through ordinary company law, it seems that a foreign court would usually accept that an entity exists, and might still ask whether the protection of its members should hold when the people and the harm are in that court's country. Nobody has fully tested whether a US or European court would respect the limited liability of a nearly anonymous Marshall Islands DAO against a local injured party. The Lido ruling suggests some judges will look at what the people actually do. That question remains open.

Follow the shell through a practical case. Suppose a DAO with a treasury in tokens wants to pay a builder in Portugal. The builder wants euros. A regulated exchange converts the tokens, and it must identify the sender under the Financial Action Task Force's Travel Rule and must check sanctions lists. If token sales promised returns, securities regulators can ask questions, and in the EU a token offered to the public needs a white paper under MiCA, the EU's crypto rules. If a sanctioned person votes or holds tokens, American members may have exposure. Developers can be reached as well. In 2023 two developers of the mixing software Tornado Cash were charged in the United States, and one, Roman Storm, was convicted on one count in 2025, even after an appeals court said the software itself could not be sanctioned. The jury could not agree on the other two charges. A retrial on those is set for 26 April 2027, and as of August 2026 he had not been sentenced and his request for acquittal was undecided.

The potential is real for governance and small for sovereignty. The strongest version is a DAO registered in a recognised state, with a real legal officer, honest disclosure to token buyers, ordinary tax compliance, and members who vote on a shared treasury and shared land. This could run schools, hold conservation land or manage services for thousands of people, and its records would be hard to falsify on the chain. Assets it holds on the blockchain are also harder for a court to freeze than a bank account, though the people holding the keys remain within reach. It would still be a company under some state's law, which can amend the statute at any time. Calling its members citizens changes nothing in the eyes of any other government.

combo-arbitration-private-law.essay:
A court needs a government behind it. Arbitration is the way around that for some disputes. Two parties agree in a contract that a private person will decide any quarrel between them. Governments have agreed to enforce the result as if a court had given it, and this is the closest thing the world has to a private legal system with state force behind it. People designing new communities therefore ask whether residents could live under a contract with a private court, enforced through the world's courts, with no government of their own. This combines a governing contract, a private court and a treaty.

The treaty is the 1958 New York Convention on foreign arbitral awards. The law it sets is clear. Under Article II, each member state must recognise a written agreement to arbitrate and send the parties to arbitration if one of them goes to court instead. Under Article III, each must enforce awards as binding. Article V gives short grounds for refusing. These include a party's incapacity, an invalid agreement, a party not given proper notice or a chance to present its case, and a tribunal that went beyond what was agreed. A court may also refuse where the subject cannot be settled by arbitration under its own law, or where enforcing would be contrary to its public policy. Those last two grounds set the outer limit. A murder cannot be arbitrated, and reading those grounds, neither can anything a state insists on deciding itself. So private law by contract can reach commerce, property use, service fees and many civil disputes, and it stops short of crime and of matters each country reserves.

The agreement is what gives it force, and that sets a second limit. Arbitration binds people who agreed. The Sulu heirs' claim shows what happens without clear consent. An arbitrator in Spain and then Paris awarded $14.92 billion against Malaysia on an 1878 paper, and French courts dismantled it, holding that no valid arbitration agreement bound Malaysia. A neighbour, a visitor or a child born in the community has signed nothing. A community contract could bind adult members and leave outsiders untouched.

Article I raises the point most relevant to places outside every country. The treaty covers awards "made in the territory of a State" other than the one where enforcement is sought. An arbitration normally has a legal home, called its seat. A commentator on blockchain justice notes that awards with no seat risk falling outside the treaty. Reading the text, it seems that an award stated to be made on a platform on the high seas, or in a self-declared state, would not be made in the territory of any member state, so a court need not treat it as a Convention award. Parties can avoid this by naming a seat in a real state, even when no one travels there. Whether a ship under a flag counts as the flag state's territory for this purpose is not answered by the text, and no ruling on it is known. The modern practice of a legal seat suggests that lawyers would simply name a land seat, which puts the project back under that state's courts. Those courts can set an award aside.

Belgium once tried removing that supervision. A 1985 law ended the setting aside of awards made in Belgium when no party had a link there. According to the arbitration lawyer Bernard Hanotiau, it deterred more parties than it attracted, and the law was repealed in 1998.

Three real designs show the range. Kleros is a blockchain protocol in which token holders serve as randomly chosen jurors. In Mexico in 2021 a court enforced an award in a lease dispute. A human arbitrator had absorbed a Kleros result into a conventional award, so the court enforced the human's award and not the protocol's ruling. Whether a pure on-chain decision by pseudonymous jurors can satisfy Article V's requirement of a fair hearing is debated and untested. Supporters point to self-enforcing transfers on the chain, which need no court when the assets are on the chain.

The Dubai International Financial Centre shows how a state's support cuts both ways. Its DIFC-LCIA centre, whose name joined the zone with the London Court of International Arbitration, was abolished by Dubai Decree 34 of 2021, effective 20 September, with its rights and duties passed to the Dubai International Arbitration Centre. Parties' old agreements were deemed valid. In Narciso v Nash in 2024 the DIFC court upheld one such clause. The zone's law survived, and a single decree still ended an institution.

Próspera goes furthest. Honduras's zone law required binding arbitration for contract and property matters. Residents sign an Agreement of Coexistence. The default provider, the Próspera Arbitration Center, is a Texas-based company with a public, court-like track producing binding precedents and rules for eviction, labour and small claims. Honduras is a party to the New York Convention. The zone's statute lets arbitration apply in some cases even if one party has not consented, and practitioners writing about it warn that this could raise questions of consent before a foreign enforcing court. Honduras's Supreme Court held the zone laws unconstitutional in September 2024. What this means for those awards has not been tested.

Scholars disagree about the historical model. Milgrom, North and Weingast wrote in 1990 that medieval merchants at the Champagne Fairs evolved a private code without state enforcement. Emily Kadens argued in 2012 that the customary law merchant is largely a myth, since widespread commercial law came from contract and statute. Stephen Sachs showed that English fair courts were neither set up by merchants nor staffed by merchant judges. The history therefore gives weak support to a law with no state.

The strongest version is a community with signed adult contracts, a named seat in a respected country, a fair procedure and limits to civil matters. That is achievable. It is a private legal order inside state law, and a state court keeps the final word.

combo-private-currency-treasury.essay:
A country usually has its own money and a central bank. A private project can try to copy this by combining a private currency, printed or digital, with a treasury kept somewhere outside its home government's easy reach. That treasury might be an account at an offshore bank, a bank the project charters for itself, or crypto held in wallets the project controls. The hope is that members can trade among themselves, that the project can pay for things, and that no government can freeze the money. Each piece has a history, and most of the history is of prosecutions.

Some of this is settled. Inside a country, that country's criminal law applies to anyone who issues money-like things there. Bernard von NotHaus minted Liberty Dollars in the United States, coins worth about $7 million in total according to the FBI. On 18 March 2011 a federal jury in North Carolina convicted him of making coins resembling US coins, of issuing and passing them as current money, and of conspiracy. The government's release said it is a federal violation to create private coin or currency systems to compete with the official coinage. Its prosecutor called such attempts a form of domestic terrorism. That case turned on metal coins resembling US money, so its reach over a clearly different token is less certain.

Digital private money met the same fate through a different law. Liberty Reserve, based in Costa Rica, let users move money with only a name, an email address and a birth date, and made no effort to verify identities. Costa Rica told it in 2009 that it needed a licence, and refused one in 2011. In May 2013 US prosecutors shut it down under the Patriot Act after an investigation across 17 countries, alleging more than $6 billion in laundering, and charged its founder Arthur Budovsky and six others. Moving offshore did not put it out of reach, because its customers and its dollars passed through places the United States could reach.

An offshore bank does not solve this. A bank in the ordinary sense needs a licence from a supervisor other banks trust, a correspondent bank to reach the world, and access to SWIFT, the messaging network banks use. A self-chartered bank has none of these. The Dominion of Melchizedek claimed to have sold about 300 bank licences, and that history is one reason compliance officers treat such licences with suspicion. A licensed bank in a low-tax country is available, and it reports account holders under the Common Reporting Standard and FATCA.

Currency codes are a smaller, real obstacle. Banks book payments using the ISO 4217 list of three-letter codes, and a new currency has no listed code. Even unrecognised governments with real economies run into exchange problems. The Somaliland shilling cannot easily be exchanged outside Somaliland, and the Transnistrian ruble can be exchanged only inside the territory. A state does not guarantee its way out of this either. The Marshall Islands passed a Sovereign Currency Act in 2018 for a national digital currency called SOV, and the International Monetary Fund opposed it. The plan later wound down. That was a recognised state, and it still could not make the idea work.

Crypto is where the law is most unsettled. Holding a token in a wallet needs no bank. Nothing about the software requires anyone's permission, and a court order has to be aimed at a person. In August 2022 the US Treasury sanctioned the mixing software Tornado Cash. On 26 November 2024 the Fifth Circuit appeals court in Van Loon held that its immutable smart contracts do not qualify as "property" under federal law, so the sanctions office lacked authority to sanction the software as such. In March 2025 the Treasury lifted those sanctions. The people were treated differently. A Dutch court sentenced developer Alexey Pertsev to 5 years and 4 months in 2024, and in 2025 a US jury found Roman Storm guilty of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, on one of three charges. The jury could not agree on the other two charges. A retrial on those is set for 26 April 2027, and as of August 2026 he had not been sentenced and his request for acquittal was undecided. So what remains open is how far software that no one controls is beyond sanctions in other courts and under other laws, and how far writing such software makes a person a money transmitter. One appeals court's reading of one statute does not answer those questions worldwide.

Follow a treasury through a real month. Suppose a community holds $20 million in stablecoins, tokens tied to the dollar, and wants to buy diesel. The fuel supplier wants dollars in a bank. A regulated exchange must identify the sender and the recipient under the Travel Rule, the international standard on money transfers, and must check sanctions lists. Stablecoin issuers can often freeze tokens at a regulator's request, and in the United States issuers now fall under the GENIUS Act of 2025. If tokens were sold to members with hope of profit, the regulators who sued over New Utopia's bonds can come back in, and EU buyers bring in the MiCA rules. Any American running the accounts is bound by US sanctions wherever they sit. Reading the money transmission cases, it seems that if the community's treasury moves funds on behalf of members, the person doing it could be treated as an unlicensed transmitter in the places members live, though the result would vary by country and has not been tested for a self-described national treasury.

The potential is modest and real. The raam, issued by the Global Country of World Peace, was accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands. A closed token that works as membership credit or a local exchange unit is a common idea, kept small and not represented as legal money. The strongest version has a token used only among members for goods and services, no promise of profit, and a reserve of ordinary money in a licensed bank or regulated custodian, with honest tax reporting by members. This gives a community an internal economy. Outside its circle, every payment still crosses into a system run by states, and the community would be a customer of that system.
